---
title: "Collecting text from a web page"
subtitle: "Scrape a saved job board without losing its source"
description: "Learn how to extract job titles and training details from structured HTML with R."
categories: [source data loading, scraping, workforce research]
---

The fictional Riverton Workforce Lab begins with six saved job postings.
A worker needs to find each job's training offers, schedule, experience
requirements, and named skills. Combining all lines without source identifiers
would make omissions and source errors difficult to find.

**Web scraping** uses code to collect information from web pages. The team will
scrape the saved page, keep the job and sentence identifiers, and examine every
record before it becomes research data. This first stage collects what the
notices say. It does not classify the sentences or generalize from them.

The lesson uses static archived HTML. The saved file contains the text within
its markup. The last sections show two page structures that the initial
extraction method cannot handle.

::: {.callout-note}
The employers, postings, and Riverton Workforce Lab are fictional. The author
wrote the HTML file for this lesson without personal information.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- explain how HTML gives parts of a page names and structure.
- select repeated job cards with rvest.
- keep source identifiers beside extracted text.
- compare scraped output with an expected fixture.
- detect a renamed class and a page whose text is not in the markup.
- describe legal, ethical, and technical checks needed before live scraping.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Begin with an archived page

Live websites change. A saved source file lets another researcher examine the
same page later. The team records the file path, size, and fingerprint before
extracting anything.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(digest)
library(rvest)

job_page_path <- "data/workforce/job-board.html"
job_page_lines <- read_lines(job_page_path)
job_page_fingerprint <- digest::digest(
  paste(job_page_lines, collapse = "\n"),
  algo = "md5",
  serialize = FALSE
)
job_page_metadata <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/job-board-metadata.csv",
  col_types = cols(
    source_file = col_character(),
    created_for_lesson = col_character(),
    retrieval_status = col_character(),
    records = col_character(),
    md5 = col_character(),
    rights_note = col_character()
  )
)
# A size read from disk counts the line endings the local copy happens to
# use, so it changes between systems. Measuring the newline-joined text, the
# same text the fingerprint covers, describes the content instead.
job_page_size <- nchar(
  paste(job_page_lines, collapse = "\n"),
  type = "bytes"
)

tibble(
  source_file = job_page_path,
  bytes = job_page_size,
  fingerprint = job_page_fingerprint
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  file.exists(job_page_path),
  identical(job_page_size, 3441L),
  identical(length(job_page_lines), 82L),
  inherits(job_page_metadata, "tbl_df"),
  identical(nrow(job_page_metadata), 1L),
  identical(
    job_page_fingerprint,
    job_page_metadata$md5
  ),
  identical(
    job_page_metadata$retrieval_status,
    "synthetic archived page"
  ),
  str_detect(
    job_page_fingerprint,
    "^[0-9a-f]{32}$"
  )
)
```

The code compares the fingerprint with a stored value. The fingerprint changes
if the archived HTML changes and can reveal an accidental edit.
It cannot prove that the postings are true or complete.

## Read the page structure

HTML uses elements such as headings, paragraphs, and lists to organize a page.
The example page places every posting inside an element whose class is
`job-card`. A **CSS selector** is a short pattern that names the elements to
collect.

```{r}
job_page <- rvest::read_html(job_page_path)
job_cards <- rvest::html_elements(
  job_page,
  ".job-card"
)

length(job_cards)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(length(job_cards), 6L)
)
```

R found six job cards. This count is the first signal that the selector matches
the archived page we expected.

## Extract one field at a time

Each card contains a job ID, posting date, title, employer, and location. The
small helper below extracts one text field from each card.

```{r}
card_text <- function(cards, selector) {
  map_chr(
    cards,
    \(card) {
      elements <- card |>
        rvest::html_elements(selector)
      stopifnot(identical(length(elements), 1L))

      elements |>
        rvest::html_text2()
    }
  )
}

jobs <- tibble(
  job_id = rvest::html_attr(
    job_cards,
    "data-job-id"
  ),
  posted = as.Date(
    rvest::html_attr(
      job_cards,
      "data-posted"
    )
  ),
  title = card_text(job_cards, ".job-title"),
  employer = card_text(job_cards, ".employer"),
  location = card_text(job_cards, ".location")
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  jobs,
  col.names = c(
    "Job ID",
    "Posted",
    "Title",
    "Employer",
    "Location"
  ),
  caption = "Six postings extracted from the archived job board",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  inherits(jobs, "tbl_df"),
  identical(jobs$job_id, sprintf("J%03d", 1:6)),
  n_distinct(jobs$job_id) == nrow(jobs),
  all(!is.na(jobs$posted)),
  all(str_length(jobs$title) > 0),
  all(str_length(jobs$employer) > 0),
  all(str_length(jobs$location) > 0),
  identical(jobs$title[1], "Data analyst trainee")
)
```

The job ID remains attached to every title. Each schedule or experience
requirement must also retain the identifier of its source posting.

## Keep sentences connected to their postings

The details in each card are list items with the class `job-detail`. We extract
them in page order and add stable sentence IDs.

```{r}
scraped_sentences <- map2(
  job_cards,
  jobs$job_id,
  \(card, job_id) {
    details <- card |>
      rvest::html_elements(".job-detail") |>
      rvest::html_text2()

    tibble(
      document_id = job_id,
      text = details
    )
  }
) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(
    sentence_id = sprintf("s%03d", row_number()),
    .before = document_id
  )

expected_sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)
expected_job_sentences <- expected_sentences |>
  filter(document_id != "F001") |>
  select(sentence_id, document_id, text) |>
  as_tibble()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  scraped_sentences |>
    slice_head(n = 8),
  col.names = c("Sentence ID", "Job ID", "Text"),
  caption = "The first eight extracted job-detail sentences",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  inherits(scraped_sentences, "tbl_df"),
  inherits(expected_job_sentences, "tbl_df"),
  identical(nrow(scraped_sentences), 22L),
  identical(
    scraped_sentences,
    expected_job_sentences
  )
)
```

All 22 sentences match the fixture in the same order. The check would stop
the build if a selector omitted, duplicated, or reordered text.

The author wrote both the HTML and expected table for this lesson.
The comparison provides a parser-behavior check, not independent truth.
A live collection would need a separate audit sample.

## When the page structure changes

The archived file preserves one page version. People can redesign a live board.
The following HTML strings illustrate two different failures of the earlier
extraction method.

The first is a redesign. The employer's new template renames `job-card` to
`posting` and moves the title into a heading.

```{r}
redesigned_html <- str_c(
  "<html><body>",
  "<div class='posting' data-job-id='J007'>",
  "<h3 class='posting-title'>Warehouse trainee</h3>",
  "<ul><li class='posting-detail'>Paid training is provided.</li></ul>",
  "</div>",
  "</body></html>"
)

redesigned_page <- rvest::read_html(redesigned_html)
old_selector_hits <- length(
  rvest::html_elements(redesigned_page, ".job-card")
)
new_selector_hits <- length(
  rvest::html_elements(redesigned_page, ".posting")
)

collect_cards <- function(page, selector, expected) {
  cards <- rvest::html_elements(page, selector)
  if (!identical(length(cards), expected)) {
    stop(
      str_c(
        "selector ",
        selector,
        " found ",
        length(cards),
        " cards; expected ",
        expected
      ),
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }

  list(
    selector = selector,
    found = length(cards),
    expected = expected,
    status = "counts agree"
  )
}

drift_error <- tryCatch(
  collect_cards(redesigned_page, ".job-card", 1L),
  error = conditionMessage
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    page = c("archived board", "redesigned page"),
    selector = ".job-card",
    cards_found = c(
      length(job_cards),
      old_selector_hits
    ),
    cards_expected = c(6L, 1L)
  ),
  col.names = c("Page", "Selector", "Cards found", "Cards expected"),
  caption = "The same selector against two versions of one site",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(old_selector_hits, 0L),
  identical(new_selector_hits, 1L),
  identical(
    drift_error,
    "selector .job-card found 0 cards; expected 1"
  ),
  identical(
    collect_cards(job_page, ".job-card", 6L)$status,
    "counts agree"
  )
)
```

Zero matches can indicate either an empty page or a selector failure.
Without an expected count, the scraper could report a redesign as a day with
no postings. A check of the expected count stops the scraper when the selector
no longer matches.

The second page's visible container has no job text. The file stores a JSON
payload in a script element. Application code could read and render that data
later. This fixture does not execute JavaScript. It separates visible markup
from embedded data.

```{r}
dynamic_html <- str_c(
  "<html><body>",
  "<div id='board'></div>",
  "<script type='application/json' id='board-data'>",
  '{"jobs": [{"id": "J008", "title": "Night stocker"}]}',
  "</script>",
  "</body></html>"
)

dynamic_page <- rvest::read_html(dynamic_html)
visible_container_text <- rvest::html_element(
  dynamic_page,
  "#board"
) |>
  rvest::html_text2()
payload_text <- rvest::html_element(
  dynamic_page,
  "#board-data"
) |>
  rvest::html_text2()

tibble(
  source = c("visible container", "script payload"),
  characters = c(
    str_length(visible_container_text),
    str_length(payload_text)
  ),
  mentions_the_job = c(
    str_detect(visible_container_text, fixed("Night stocker")),
    str_detect(payload_text, fixed("Night stocker"))
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    length(rvest::html_elements(dynamic_page, ".job-card")),
    0L
  ),
  identical(visible_container_text, ""),
  str_detect(payload_text, fixed("Night stocker")),
  !str_detect(visible_container_text, fixed("Night stocker"))
)
```

The container holds no characters. The job title exists only in the embedded
script payload, which rvest can read as text but does not render into the
container.

This example includes the payload in the file. Many sites request data
separately after loading the initial page. Their saved initial HTML may contain
no text to extract. An HTML parser cannot recover a response that the archive
does not contain.

Three collection methods differ in cost and guarantees.
First, search for a documented API that returns the data under stated terms.
The page's underlying data request may also accept direct calls.
Direct calls can be faster but depend on an interface that the provider may
change.

A headless browser runs the page as a browser would. R can control one through
chromote, and Python can use Playwright or Selenium.
This is the general solution and the most expensive of these methods to run
and maintain.

Record the collection method. Text from a rendered page and text from a saved
file are different evidence. Readers need to know which method produced the
reported numbers.


## A saved page is still incomplete evidence

The archived HTML shows what was captured, not every posting that existed.
Before scraping a live site, the team must examine:

1. the site's terms and robots policy.
2. whether collection is lawful and expected in the relevant jurisdiction.
3. whether personal or sensitive information appears.
4. permitted request frequency.
5. whether JavaScript loads page content later.
6. the dates, filters, and geographic limits of the results.
7. how the saved HTML and retrieval time will be preserved.

The Robots Exclusion Protocol communicates crawler preferences. It is not a
grant of legal permission, and permission does not settle every ethical
question. A public page can still contain information that should not be
collected or republished.

## What to remember

- Scraping converts page structure into data. It does not establish that the
  data is true or representative.
- Archive the source. Record its collection date.
- Keep source IDs attached to extracted text.
- Assert expected counts and content so selector failures cannot return zero
  rows without an error.
- Zero matches and an empty page look identical without an expected count.
- Some pages load text separately from the saved markup. An HTML parser cannot
  extract text absent from its input.
- Examine terms, rate limits, privacy, and research ethics before live
  collection.

The team can examine 22 sentences with their source identifiers from the six
notices. The table excludes one source, a fictional training flyer saved as an
image. That source requires OCR instead of HTML extraction.
Preserve the image. Examine the extracted wording before using it.
